label: Philosophy + psychology
reader: for a reader who picked philosophy and psychology
subject: Three good finds, just for you.
preheader: Wonder, other minds, and the overlooked art of being helped.
intro: Today’s thread: staying open to what you haven’t figured out. Three finds for a mind interested in other minds.

stories.title: When curiosity becomes another scroll.
stories.original: To benefit from wonder, make sure you’ve got the genuine kind
stories.alt: A hiker with a large backpack on a ridge above misty mountains.
stories.credit: Simon Townsley / Panos Pictures · via Psyche
stories.summary: Can collecting fascinating facts become its own kind of distraction? Lisa Sideris distinguishes lasting wonder from a restless appetite for the next mystery. Once a puzzle is solved, that appetite moves on. More durable wonder can tolerate an unfinished explanation and let an encounter change our perspective. Her essay offers an unexpectedly sharp question for an internet full of interesting things: are we becoming more receptive, or merely consuming more novelty?
stories.note: For your interest in attention: even curiosity can become a feed.

stories.title: Your mind’s eye isn’t everyone’s.
stories.alt: Close-up of a person’s face and ear in low light.
stories.summary: Picture an apple. For some people, that request produces a vivid image; for others, no mental picture appears. Gary Lupyan explores these hidden differences in imagery, inner speech and memory, and why we so often assume our own experience is universal. The striking implication goes beyond perception: someone may respond differently because the situation actually feels different to them. Understanding another person can begin with asking what their experience is like.
stories.note: For your interest in psychology—and designing for minds unlike your own.

stories.title: The overlooked art of being helped.
stories.original: How Will the Miracle Happen Today?

panel.label: A QUESTION TO TAKE INTO TODAY

stories.summary: Kevin Kelly remembers hitchhiking to work and accepting remarkable hospitality while travelling. His unusual focus is the receiving side of generosity: the vulnerability of letting someone help you. He calls that recipient a “kindee” and reflects on gratitude as a way of meeting the world. This is a personal, spiritual interpretation of his experiences, rather than a promise that kindness always arrives. The invitation is to notice the gifts we struggle to accept.
stories.note: A warmer place to land: you don’t have to earn every good thing.

label: Product design
reader: for a reader who picked product design, typography and craft
interests: SAMPLE EDITION · TYPOGRAPHY + CRAFT AND PROCESS
subject: Three good finds, just for you.
preheader: Type, craft, and the decisions nobody notices until they are wrong.

stories.title: Solemn is easy. Serious is hard.
stories.alt: Image from TED: Great design is serious (not solemn)
stories.summary: Scher borrows a distinction from Russell Baker — solemn is easy, serious is hard — and applies it to a 35-year career at Pentagram. Solemn work is correct, approved and safe; serious work happens spontaneously, often out of innocence or arrogance, and is usually imperfect. She counts four genuinely serious moments in her own career, including the Citibank logo drawn on a napkin, and is honest that the rest was competent solemnity. A good corrective if your process has become entirely process.
stories.note: For your interest in craft and process.

stories.title: A typeface that cannot stop meaning something
stories.short:
A typeface that cannot
stop meaning something
stories.summary: A sign on a Dresden bus, set in blackletter, is enough to start an argument about who counts as German. The episode traces Fraktur from medieval scribes economising on quill strokes, through its slow loss to Roman type, to the Nazis adopting it and then abruptly banning it in 1941. What you get is a working demonstration that a typeface carries history whether or not the designer intends it, which is worth having in mind the next time a font feels merely decorative.

stories.title: Resilient Web Design, Chapter 2: Materials
stories.alt: Image from resilientwebdesign.com: Resilient Web Design, Chapter 2: Materials
stories.summary: Keith explains why the web's materials behave unlike anything designers came from: HTML that renders despite errors, CSS that ignores what it does not understand, and the layering that lets a page survive missing pieces. Progressive enhancement follows from the material rather than being imposed on it. Short, beautifully written, and the clearest explanation of why the web is so hard to break.

What the machines do

interests: SAMPLE EDITION · HOW MODELS WORK + SOFTWARE CRAFT
subject: Three good finds, just for you.
preheader: Models, software craft, and the arguments underneath both.
intro: Today: how models work and software craft.

stories.title: Looking inside a network, neuron by neuron
stories.short:
Looking inside a
network, neuron by neuron
stories.original: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
stories.by: Chris Olah, Nick Cammarata, Ludwig Schubert, Gabriel Goh, Michael Petrov, and Shan Carter
stories.alt: Image from Distill: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
stories.summary: The opening paper of the circuits programme argues that neural networks can be studied like cells under a microscope. Features are directions in activation space, circuits are the weighted connections between them, and both can be read off a trained vision model. Curve detectors and high-low frequency detectors are traced in detail. It is the founding document of mechanistic interpretability, and it stays concrete throughout.
stories.note: For your interest in how models work.

stories.title: Simple is not the same as easy
stories.short:
Simple is not
the same as easy
stories.alt: Image from Strange Loop: Simple Made Easy
stories.summary: Hickey separates two words we use interchangeably. Simple is objective — one fold, one braid, nothing twisted together. Easy is relative to you: near at hand, familiar, already installed. Most of what we choose in software is chosen for easiness, and the complexity we pay for it is not visible until the system is large. He then goes construct by construct — state, objects, inheritance, ORMs, conditionals — naming what each one complects. The talk that put 'complect' into working vocabularies.
stories.note: For your interest in software craft.

stories.title: Search, planning, and the limits of scaling
stories.short:
Search, planning, and
the limits of scaling
stories.original: Demis Hassabis — Scaling, superhuman AIs, AlphaZero atop LLMs, AlphaFold
stories.alt: Image from Dwarkesh Podcast: Demis Hassabis — Scaling, superhuman AIs, AlphaZero atop LLMs, AlphaFold
stories.summary: The head of Google DeepMind on why scaling is still, in his words, an art form rather than an engineering discipline, and on what happens when you put AlphaZero-style search and planning on top of a language model. Patel presses him on timelines, on whether an intelligence explosion is a thing you can steer, on keeping model weights out of the hands of states that want them, and on how Gemini was actually trained. A transcript is posted alongside if you would rather read it.
